Ulysses. James Joyce's 1922 modernist masterpiece follows Leopold Bloom through Dublin on June 16, 1904, mirroring Homer's Odyssey in the span of a single day. Famous for its experimental stream-of-consciousness technique, fragmented narrative, and linguistic innovation, it transformed what literature could be and remains one of the most influential—and challenging—novels ever written.

Published in 1922, the novel was initially banned in many countries for obscenity. It represents the apex of modernist fiction. Structured as a paralleled journey, the wanderings of Leopold Bloom and Stephen Dedalus through Dublin echo Odysseus's voyage home, collapsing epic into urban dailiness.

The novel employs stream-of-consciousness narration—the unfiltered interior monologue of its characters—as its primary narrative mode. This captures thought exactly as it occurs, including fragmented, digressive, and even ungrammatical phrasing. The Proteus and Circe episodes are among the most formally audacious, shifting styles, scripts, lists, and modes of address within a single chapter.

Bloom and Stephen represent opposite poles: the former a practical, sensual, compassionate everyman, the latter a young artist-intellectual struggling with exile and identity. The novel contains no chapters or traditional narrative breaks—it is divided instead into eighteen episodes, each with its own stylistic signature and sometimes a Homeric parallel. The novel is famous for Molly Bloom's soliloquy, a forty-page interior monologue by Bloom's wife that is virtually unpunctuated and captures raw female desire and bodily consciousness. Ulysses exemplifies modernism and revolutionized the capacity of fiction to explore consciousness with radical formal experimentation.
